R1.text: ACOG recommends that obstetricians be prepared to counsel patients on the benefits and risks of psychopharmacotherapy for perinatal mental health conditions when clinically indicated.

R2.text: ACOG recommends that obstetricians initiate psychopharmacotherapy for perinatal depression or anxiety disorders, refer patients to appropriate behavioral health resources when indicated, or both.

R3.text: ACOG recommends that a validated screening tool be used to monitor for response to treatment or remission of depression or anxiety symptoms. If clinically indicated, the pharmacotherapy dosage should be up-titrated, with the goal of remission of depressive and anxiety symptoms.

R4.text: ACOG recommends that treatment for perinatal mood and anxiety disorders be equitably available and accessible to all pregnant and postpartum individuals.

R5.text: ACOG recommends against withholding or discontinuing medications for mental health conditions due to pregnancy or lactation status alone.

GPP1.text: Use Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs as a resource for management and treatment guidance for individuals with mental health conditions.

R6.text: ACOG recommends that psychotherapy be considered a first-line treatment for mild-to-moderate perinatal depression.

R7.text: ACOG recommends that SSRIs be used as first-line pharmacotherapy for perinatal depression. SNRIs are reasonable alternatives. Pharmacotherapy should be individualized based on prior response to therapy (if applicable). If there is no pharmacotherapy history, sertraline or escitalopram are reasonable first-line medications.

R8.text: ACOG recommends consideration of brexanolone administration in the postpartum period for moderate-to-severe perinatal depression with onset in the third trimester or within 4 weeks postpartum (balancing rapid onset against access, cost, breastfeeding, inpatient monitoring, and lack of efficacy data beyond 30 days).

R9.text: ACOG recommends that SSRIs be used as first-line psychopharmacotherapy for perinatal anxiety. SNRIs are reasonable alternatives. Pharmacotherapy should be individualized based on prior response to therapy (if applicable). If there is no pharmacotherapy history, sertraline or escitalopram are reasonable first-line medications.

R10.text: ACOG recommends that benzodiazepines be avoided or prescribed sparingly as a treatment for perinatal anxiety.

R11.text: ACOG recommends against discontinuing mood stabilizers, except for valproate, during pregnancy due to the risk of recurrence or exacerbation of mood symptoms.

R12.text: ACOG recommends against valproate as a first-line treatment for bipolar disorder. Valproate should be avoided in pregnancy because reasonable alternatives usually can be identified.

R13.text: ACOG recommends that pregnant individuals using antipsychotic medications undergo screening for gestational diabetes mellitus, consistent with standard prenatal care.

R14.text: ACOG recommends that pregnant patients taking lithium in the first trimester receive a detailed ultrasound examination in the second trimester.

GPP2.text: It is imperative that lithium dosing be monitored during pregnancy and postpartum.

GPP3.text: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. Treatment options within the scope of obstetricians while awaiting psychiatric assessment include sedating antipsychotics such as olanzapine or haloperidol, which can be used with benzodiazepines such as lorazepam; if haloperidol is used, benztropine or diphenhydramine should be given to prevent extrapyramidal symptoms and dystonia.
